```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(baggr)

baggr::baggr_theme_update(text = element_text(family = "mono"))
```



## baggr

_baggr_ (Bayesian aggregator) is a new R package for Bayesian meta-analysis models that uses Stan

Our goals: 

1. Implement all basic meta-analysis models and tools
2. Focus on accessibility, model criticism and comparison
3. Help people avoid basic mistakes
4. Keep the framework flexible and extend to more models

(Probably) _not_ our goal:

5. Build a package for people who already build their models in Stan

_baggr_ beta is available on [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=baggr) and [GitHub](https://github.com/wwiecek/baggr)




## Basic model of meta-analysis is simple...

After Rubin (1981)\footnote{Rubin, Donald B. "Estimation in Parallel Randomized Experiments". Journal of Educational Statistics 6, no. 4 (1981): 377–401.}

* Assume only aggregate data ($y$, $se$) are known ($y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\tau_i, se_i)$)
    + We treat $se_i$ as fixed (works OK with big samples)
* Hierarchical model: $\tau_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\tau, \sigma)$
    +  $\sigma = 0$ is "full pooling", $\sigma = \infty$ is "no pooling"
    + Fixed and random effects in medical stats
    + Typically it's more sensible to start with $0 < \sigma < \infty$
    + Note how the amount of heterogeneity across $i$'s will be controlled by $\sigma$ prior


## ...but it gets more complicated fast

* Continuous, categorical data
* Meta-analysis of means (summary data) 
* Meta-regression
* Individual-level data (or a mix of summary and individual)
* Modeling more parameters (mixture data, variances, quantiles)
* Dealing with small samples (e.g. chemical risk assessment)
* Model-based meta-analysis (drug development)
* Network meta-analysis / ITC (health technology assessment)

Techniques, terminology, _motivations_ and even software are very domain-specific



## Example (8 schools!)

We use a familiar summary-level dataset from Rubin (1981). Individual-level data works just as well.


\small

```{r, echo = T}
library(baggr)
schools
```



## _baggr_  syntax example: simple model workflow

\tiny 

```{r, eval = T, include = F, cache = T}
# Fitting function is baggr()
fit <- baggr(schools, model = "rubin", pooling = "partial",
             prior_hypermean = normal(0, 25), prior_hypersd = uniform(0, 100))

# Automatic prior choice, automatic model choice (with prompts):
eff_lab <- "mean SAT improvement"
niter <- 1e04 #to make it a bit smoother in slides
fit_c <- baggr(schools, prior_hypersd = cauchy(0, 50), effect = eff_lab,
               iter = niter)
fit_n <- baggr(schools, prior_hypersd = normal(0, 10), effect = eff_lab,
               iter = niter)
fit_u <- baggr(schools, prior_hypersd = uniform(0, 100),
                        prior_hypermean = normal(-5, 10), effect = eff_lab,
               iter = niter)

# Plot results for one model, making use of bayesplot
baggr_theme_update(text = element_text(family = "mono"))
plot(fit_c, style = "areas", hyper = TRUE, order = TRUE)

# Compare fit to data
bgc <- baggr_compare("Cauchy" = fit_c, "Normal" = fit_n, "Uniform" = fit_u)
bgc; plot(bgc)
# Compare posterior predictive distribution (note ggplot)
effect_plot("Cauchy" = fit_c, "Normal" = fit_n, "Uniform" = fit_u) + xlim(-10, 30)

# Compare the impact of different prior choices
bgc_pooling <- baggr_compare(schools, prior_hypersd = normal(0, 10), what = "pooling")
plot(bgc_pooling)

# Use LOO cross-validation to choose between partial & full pooling
loo_p <- loocv(schools, pooling = "partial")
loo_f <- loocv(schools, pooling = "full")
loo_compare(loo_p, loo_f)
```

```{r, eval = F, include = T}
# Fitting function is baggr()
fit <- baggr(schools, model = "rubin", pooling = "partial",
             prior_hypermean = normal(0, 25), prior_hypersd = uniform(0, 100))

# Semi-automatic prior choice, automatic model choice (with prompts):
eff_lab <- "mean SAT improvement"
fit_c <- baggr(schools, prior_hypersd = cauchy(0, 50), effect = eff_lab)
fit_n <- baggr(schools, prior_hypersd = normal(0, 10), effect = eff_lab)
fit_u <- baggr(schools, prior_hypersd = uniform(0, 100),
                        prior_hypermean = normal(-5, 10), effect = eff_lab)

# Plot results for one model, making use of bayesplot
baggr_theme_update(text = element_text(family = "mono"))
plot(fit_c, style = "areas", hyper = TRUE, order = TRUE)

# Compare fit to data
bgc <- baggr_compare("Cauchy" = fit_c, "Normal" = fit_n, "Uniform" = fit_u)
bgc; plot(bgc)
# Compare posterior predictive distribution (note ggplot)
effect_plot("Cauchy" = fit_c, "Normal" = fit_n, "Uniform" = fit_u) + xlim(-10, 30)

# Compare the impact of different prior choices
bgc_pooling <- baggr_compare(schools, prior_hypersd = normal(0, 10), what = "pooling")
plot(bgc_pooling)

# Use LOO cross-validation to choose between partial & full pooling
loo_p <- loocv(schools, pooling = "partial")
loo_f <- loocv(schools, pooling = "full")
loo_compare(loo_p, loo_f)
```

Additional commands: 

```{r, echo = T, eval = F}
treatment_effect(fit)
group_effects(fit)
effect_draw(fit)
forest_plot(fit)
pooling(fit)
```



## Going beyond the simple use cases

Already included in the new release (v0.7, July 2020):

* Models with many parameters (quantiles, mixtures, effects on means & variances)
* Running models on individual-level data
* Including covariates (meta-regression or individual-level)
* Working with binary data (rare events, L'Abbe and bubble plots)
* Extra summaries, transforms and plots of data
* Tutorial vignettes



## How to make the tool better? Our 5 questions

How to...

* Improve syntax and/or make it more flexible
* Reach more users
* Understand who does and who doesn't need help
* Give more technical users means of extending their models
* Connect more to Stan ecosystem (e.g. `bayesplot`)

Each of these areas is where feedback from Stan community is especially valuable
